title: The EU Commission has been the victim of a cyberattack carried out using AI
content:
Brussels – The European Commission has been hit by a malicious cyberattack that has affected several of its internal departments. The EU executive’s spokesperson responsible for digital and technological sovereignty issues, Thomas Regnier, confirmed certain press previews during the daily press conference in Brussels today (19 November). The incident was detected on 22 October and confirmed on 26 October, following initial investigations. According to the EU Commission, artificial intelligence tools were also reportedly used to carry out the attack.
“The Commission has recently taken the necessary measures in response to a malicious cyber campaign that was detected. As a precautionary and preventative measure, we have temporarily disabled several applications, most of which have since been restored,” explained the spokesperson. Brussels has also launched an investigation in close cooperation with CERT-EU, the European Union agency responsible for the cybersecurity of the institutions, and with the European Data Protection Supervisor.
The services affected include Sysper, the platform used by Commission staff to view payslips, request leave, and record hours worked, and MyPMO, the system for managing medical expense reimbursements. According to press reports, both services remained unavailable for around ten days before becoming operational again at the start of the week. Other applications had been suspended as a precautionary measure.
“At this stage of the investigation, we have not found any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole,” the spokesperson clarified regarding the possible access to confidential information by staff members. However, the EU executive has not provided a quantification of the scale of the attack, describing it as a campaign comprising a series of incidents. Furthermore, no ransom demands have been reported.
One finding to emerge from the initial investigations concerns the use of artificial intelligence tools. According to the spokesperson, the perpetrators of the campaign are said to have “used a publicly available AI tool to identify potential vulnerabilities in IT systems.”.According to CERT-EU, ARTEX was reportedly used – an AI-based software programme designed to identify system vulnerabilities.
There was, however, no indication as to the identity of those responsible or the possible origin of the attack. “As regards attributing responsibility, I do not wish to comment: the investigation is ongoing,” the spokesperson clarified, assuring that the Commission is taking all necessary countermeasures based on the evidence gathered.
The government finally pointed out that it had presented a plan dedicated to cybersecurity and artificial intelligence in July, emphasising that tools based on these technologies can also be used to identify cyber vulnerabilities. “No one is immune” to cyber attacks, the spokesperson concluded.

report.summary: The European Commission confirmed an AI-assisted cyber campaign hit several internal systems, prompting temporary app shutdowns and a CERT-EU investigation.
report.background: The incident comes as EU institutions rely on interconnected internal platforms for payroll, leave, timekeeping, and expense claims. The Commission detected the malicious campaign on 22 October and confirmed it on 26 October, then temporarily disabled several applications as a precaution. Sysper and MyPMO were reportedly unavailable for about ten days. Brussels is investigating with CERT-EU, the EU agency for institutional cybersecurity, and the European Data Protection Supervisor. The case reflects a broader trend: AI tools are lowering the cost of vulnerability discovery, while public bodies face rising pressure to secure legacy and cloud-based systems. The Commission says it presented a cybersecurity and AI plan in July, acknowledging that AI can serve both defense and attack.
key_points: Detection and response: the Commission detected the campaign on 22 October and confirmed it on 26 October. It disabled several applications as a precaution, most of which were restored. Sysper, used for payslips, leave, and time records, and MyPMO, for medical reimbursements, were reportedly down for around ten days.

AI-assisted attack: investigators say the perpetrators used a publicly available AI tool to identify potential vulnerabilities in IT systems. CERT-EU reportedly pointed to ARTEX, an AI-based vulnerability-identification programme. This shows how accessible AI can speed up reconnaissance and weakness discovery.

Scope and data risk: the Commission says it has not found evidence of a data breach affecting staff as a whole. It has not quantified the attack, describing it as a campaign of incidents. No ransom demand has been reported, and attribution remains unclear while the investigation continues.

Policy implications: Brussels says no one is immune to cyberattacks and has presented a cybersecurity and AI plan. The case highlights the dual-use nature of AI security tools: the same capabilities that help defenders find flaws can help attackers locate weak points.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the incident reinforces that vulnerability-discovery models and agents are dual-use. Expect more scrutiny of abuse monitoring, access controls, and logging for security-oriented AI tools. For developers, the lesson is to treat internal HR and finance apps as high-value targets: maintain asset inventories, patch quickly, enforce least privilege, and run continuous dependency and vulnerability scanning. For regular users, the immediate effect was service disruption rather than confirmed widespread data exposure, but the case shows how AI can make public-sector attacks faster and more targeted. Transparency about scope, safeguards, and recovery timelines will be important for maintaining trust.
report.tools: Watch CERT-EU advisories and the reported ARTEX AI vulnerability-identification tool. For hands-on defensive testing, open-source options include Nuclei for template-based vulnerability checks, OWASP ZAP for web app scanning, OpenVAS/Greenbone for network vulnerability management, Trivy for container and dependency scanning, and Semgrep for static code analysis. Use them only on systems you are authorised to test, and pair scanning with patch management and monitoring.
